## S02 From Quartz to a Chip  (0:36.24–1:14.75)

- 0:36.24 picture-only pre-roll 0.30 s
- 0:36.69–0:40.78 Our journey begins with silicon, found in materials such as quartz.
- 0:41.24–0:44.55 But ordinary sand cannot simply become a processor.
- 0:45.11–0:53.82 Silicon must be refined to extraordinary purity, grown into a single crystal, sliced into thin wafers and polished.
- 0:54.24–0:57.50 Then microscopic structures are created on the wafer.
- 0:57.90–1:01.75 At their heart are transistors, tiny electrical switches.
- 1:02.45–1:03.53 One switch is simple.

## S03 The Precision Problem  (1:14.75–2:14.71)

- 1:14.75 picture-only pre-roll 0.30 s
- 1:15.12–1:17.50 Why can't every country make advanced chips?
- 1:18.20–1:23.49 Because the process demands extraordinary precision, repeated layer after layer.
- 1:23.89–1:28.17 In photolithography, a light-sensitive coating is applied to the wafer.
- 1:28.59–1:31.07 Light transfers a carefully designed pattern.
- 1:31.48–1:37.26 The material is developed, selected areas are etched and new layers are added.
- 1:37.66–1:41.22 The wafer passes through many specialised stages.
- 1:42.23–1:45.43 all requiring precise alignment and control.
- 1:45.44 **HOLD 1.00 s** — particle freeze, near-silence
- 1:46.45–1:50.44 Now imagine a microscopic particle landing on the surface.
- 1:51.02–1:57.99 At this scale, contamination can damage tiny features and reduce the number of usable chips.
- 1:58.65–2:08.80 That is why fabrication plants need controlled clean rooms, specialised machines, pure chemicals and gases, and deep technical expertise.
- 2:09.30–2:14.40 Even after fabrication, the chip must be cut, packaged, tested, and verified.
- 2:14.41 picture-only tail 0.30 s
